summary: Defines internationalized domain names and the IDNA mechanism, which lets domain names use non-ASCII characters from Unicode while representing them using ASCII so existing DNS software keeps working. It was replaced by RFC 5890 and RFC 5891.

plainLanguage.summary: Web addresses used to be limited to plain English letters. IDNA lets people use their own alphabets by quietly converting them to a plain form. It was later replaced by RFC 5890 and RFC 5891.

questions: what does xn-- mean in a domain name
how do internationalized domain names work
subtitle: How applications can use non-ASCII characters in domain names while the DNS keeps seeing plain ASCII.

tldr.problem: Domain names were limited to ASCII characters, with no standard way to use other scripts, and changing every DNS server and resolver was not realistic.
tldr.mechanism: Applications convert each non-ASCII label to an ASCII form that starts with the prefix xn-- (ToASCII) and convert it back for display (ToUnicode), using Nameprep and Punycode. No change to the DNS is needed.
tldr.outcome: Only applications need updating, and existing infrastructure keeps working. RFC 3490 has since been obsoleted by RFC 5890 and RFC 5891.

today: RFC 3490 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 5890 and RFC 5891, so those define internationalized domain names now.

sections.title: The Idea Behind IDNA
sections.content:
Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) lets applications use certain ASCII labels, starting with a special prefix, to stand for non-ASCII labels. Lower layers do not need to know. IDNA does not depend on changes to DNS servers, resolvers or protocol elements, because the existing ASCII name service is enough.

Applications are not required to conform, but if an application wants non-ASCII characters in domain names, IDNA is the only currently defined option. Adding it means changing the application only. IDNA uses the Unicode character repertoire, with some restrictions.

The RFC is open about its limits. The DNS still offers exact-match lookup, and IDNA does not solve language and script issues such as mixed traditional and simplified Chinese, or visually similar names that a person might mistype from a business card.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of rebuilding the whole phone book, IDNA only changes how you write the names before you look them up.

sections.title: Labels, ACE and Domain Name Slots
sections.content:
A label is one part of a domain name, for example www in www.example.com. An ACE label (ASCII Compatible Encoding) is an ASCII rendering of an internationalized label. Every ACE label begins with the ACE prefix. ACE labels are unsuitable for display to users.

A domain name slot is a protocol element or function argument explicitly designated for carrying a domain name, such as the QNAME field of a DNS query. A slot is IDN-aware if it is designated to carry internationalized names, and IDN-unaware otherwise, which includes anything specified before IDNA. Plain text that merely contains a domain name is not a slot.

Two labels are equivalent if and only if their ASCII forms from ToASCII match using a case-insensitive ASCII comparison. This extends the old rule that upper and lower case are the same.
sections.plainLanguage: A slot is a box on a form that is only meant for a web address. IDNA makes sure that old boxes only ever get the plain-letter version.

sections.title: The Four Requirements
sections.content:
Conformance means following four rules. First, wherever dots separate labels, four characters must be recognized as dots: U+002E, U+3002, U+FF0E and U+FF61. Second, a name placed in an IDN-unaware slot MUST contain only ASCII, which is done by applying ToASCII to each label.

Third, ACE labels obtained from slots SHOULD be hidden from users when the environment can handle the non-ACE form, unless the ACE form is requested. Fourth, labels match if and only if they are equivalent, as described above, and names match if their labels match.

IDNA applies to all domain names in all slots unless excluded. It does not apply to names in resource records whose CLASS is not IN. It also does not let other data stored in domain labels, such as an email local part, use non-ASCII characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Treat the four different dot characters as dots, send only plain letters to old systems, show people their own alphabet, and compare names by their plain-letter form.

sections.title: ToASCII, ToUnicode and the xn-- Prefix
sections.content:
The ToASCII operation takes one label and, if it has non-ASCII code points, runs Nameprep, then encodes it with Punycode and prepends the ACE prefix. It also checks that the result has 1 to 63 code points. ToASCII can fail, and then the name cannot be used as an internationalized domain name. It never changes an all-ASCII label, and applying it twice has the same effect as once.

The ToUnicode operation reverses this: it removes the prefix, decodes with Punycode, and checks the result by applying ToASCII again. ToUnicode never fails; on any error it returns the original input.

The ACE prefix is xn-- in any capitalization, which is two alphanumeric ASCII characters followed by two hyphen-minuses. An example ACE label is xn--de-jg4avhby1noc0d. Nameprep and Punycode are both mandatory for implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: ToASCII is writing your name in a safe code that starts with xn--. ToUnicode is reading the code back into your real name.

sections.title: Applications, Resolvers and DNS Servers
sections.content:
IDNA lives entirely inside applications, as a shim between the application and the resolver library, or just before a name is written into a DNS zone. Applications may accept and show names in any character set. They MUST run ToASCII on labels they pass to the resolver library, and labels coming back are ASCII, in ACE form where needed.

DNS servers MUST use the ACE form for internationalized labels, so everything they serve is ASCII. Because of how ToASCII and ToUnicode are designed, there is only one ASCII encoding for a given name. With DNSSEC, the ASCII name is what gets signed and validated, not the Unicode form.

If an application cannot display every character of a decoded name, it SHOULD show the ACE form rather than replacement characters. The RFC also notes that longer IDNs may increase root server bandwidth slightly and push more queries from UDP to TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the program on your computer does the translating. The internet's address book keeps seeing the plain-letter code and never has to change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security on the Internet partly relies on DNS, and security suffers if a user typing one internationalized name can be connected to different servers because of different interpretations. If applications transcode from a local character set to Unicode differently, they could contact different servers.

Implementations MUST NOT use more recent normalization tables than the one this RFC references. To reduce confusion between visually similar characters, the RFC suggests visual indications when a name mixes scripts, and notes that zone administrators may restrict registrations to limit homographs. Comparisons against privileged domains must use the proper equivalence rule. Existing labels that start with the ACE prefix and would be altered by ToUnicode automatically become ACE labels.
sections.plainLanguage: Look-alike letters can trick people into visiting the wrong site. Everyone must translate names the same way, and programs should warn about mixed alphabets.
